title: THE ARGUMENT
headline:
THE
ORDER
subtitle: What Jallianwala Bagh was really fighting over
dek: A garden, a banned meeting, and a general who decided that the Empire's authority was worth more than the people in front of him. The question is not only what happened. It is what the state did with the truth afterwards.
eyeopener: A walled garden is not a battlefield. That is the point. On 13 April 1919, thousands of people walked into a space with five narrow exits to listen to speeches and mark a festival. A general blocked the main way out and ordered his men to fire into the crowd. The Empire did not call it a massacre. It called it a disturbance. The words were part of the fight.

labels.contextDek: Eleven turns in the political fight. The firing did not come from nowhere; it came from a legal order, a frightened city, and an army trained to see a crowd as a threat.
labels.debateDek: Seven questions that still start fights. Each one gives the strongest case on both sides, then names the fact that makes the argument uncomfortable.
labels.sourcesDek: Every factual claim in the timeline points here. Interpretations are arguments, not facts. A source can be wrong; a source can also be improved.

context.title: The wartime emergency
context.text: The Defence of India Act gave the colonial government sweeping powers to detain people without ordinary trial. Wartime emergency rule normalised the idea that the Raj could suspend the law when it felt threatened.

context.title: The Rowlatt Act
context.text: The Rowlatt Act extended emergency-style powers into peacetime. It allowed detention without trial and trial without a jury. Indian members of the legislature opposed it; the government passed it anyway.

context.title: Two leaders arrested
context.text: In Amritsar, the police arrested Dr Saifuddin Kitchlew and Dr Satyapal. A crowd gathered to protest. The arrests turned a legal dispute into a confrontation on the street.

context.title: A city on edge
context.text: Protests spread and violence broke out. Mobs attacked banks, the railway station and mission property; several Europeans were killed. Dyer was given command in Amritsar and imposed a curfew.

context.title: Baisakhi — and the notice
context.text: Baisakhi brought pilgrims and visitors into Amritsar. Dyer issued a proclamation banning public meetings, but the notice was not widely read. A crowd gathered in Jallianwala Bagh, a walled garden near the Golden Temple.

context.title: The firing
context.text: Dyer arrived about an hour after the meeting began, with fifty soldiers, and blocked the main exit. He gave no warning to disperse. The troops fired into the densest part of the crowd, toward the narrow exits, for about ten minutes. Dyer later reported 1,650 rounds.

context.title: The well and the wounded
context.text: The official inquiry counted 379 dead and more than 1,200 wounded; other estimates were higher. Some of the dead were recovered from a well inside the garden. A plaque at the site says 120 bodies were taken from it.

context.title: The Hunter Commission
context.text: The Hunter Commission criticised Dyer's decision to fire without warning and his failure to stop. It did not prosecute him. He was relieved of his command and barred from employment in India, but never tried for murder.

context.title: Non-cooperation
context.text: The massacre helped turn the Congress toward mass non-cooperation. Gandhi and the Congress built a campaign around boycott, resignation and non-payment. It was not the only cause, but it changed what many people believed the Raj was willing to do.

context.title: Udham Singh
context.text: In London, Udham Singh shot Sir Michael O'Dwyer, the former Lieutenant Governor of Punjab, in revenge for the massacre. Singh was tried and executed. The act became a symbol of the argument that the Empire understood only force.

context.title: Regret, not apology
context.text: On the centenary, Britain expressed deep regret for the massacre. It did not issue a formal apology. The distinction matters to the families and to the political argument about what a state owes after it kills.

debates.question: Was the firing a massacre, or a legitimate response to a riot?
debates.hook: This is the argument the Empire made in 1919, and it is still worth stating clearly — because the strongest version of it is also the easiest to defeat.
debates.stakes: If a state can call an unarmed crowd a riot, it can describe almost any killing as order restored. The words decide what counts as evidence.
caseFor: Dyer claimed the meeting was part of a conspiracy to overthrow British rule, and that a larger rebellion was imminent.
A curfew and a ban on public meetings had been imposed; the crowd was breaking the order, and the city had already seen violence.
A commander on the ground may have believed that a show of force would prevent a wider uprising and save lives.
caseAgainst: The crowd was in a walled garden with narrow exits; Dyer blocked the main one and gave no warning to disperse.
The troops fired into the densest part of the crowd, continued for about ten minutes, and fired 1,650 rounds — far beyond what was needed to disperse a meeting.
The Hunter Commission unanimously condemned Dyer's conduct, finding that continuing to fire as long as he did was a grave error; it did not accept that the threat justified the duration.
debates.uncomfortable: The defense does not need Dyer to be a monster. It needs only the claim that a colonial officer could decide, alone, that a crowd had forfeited the right to live.
debates.whatWouldChange: Evidence that the crowd was armed, that a warning was given, that the firing stopped as soon as the crowd began to leave, or that a specific order authorized lethal force.

debates.question: Was Dyer solely responsible, or was the system?
debates.hook: The easiest story is a single bad officer. The harder story is a government that made him possible, then let him retire.
debates.stakes: If the blame stops at one man, the next officer learns that the system will protect him. If the blame becomes only 'the system', no one is responsible for the trigger.
caseFor: Dyer chose to march into the Bagh, chose the position, chose not to warn, and chose to keep firing.
He told the commission he had gone to the Bagh with the deliberate intention of opening fire if a crowd was assembled, and that he could have dispersed it without firing but did not.
The order to fire was his; no superior ordered him to shoot into the crowd.
caseAgainst: Dyer was operating inside a colonial command culture that treated Indian protest as sedition and had already normalized emergency detention.
The Punjab government and the Viceroy's administration defended him for months; the House of Commons debate became a vote on the Empire's conduct, not only on one officer.
No senior official was prosecuted, and the state pensioned the officer whose command ended in a garden full of bodies.
debates.uncomfortable: The system did not need to order the killing. It needed to produce a man who believed the killing was administration.
debates.whatWouldChange: Evidence that Dyer acted against explicit orders, or that a superior specifically directed him to use lethal force; or evidence that the system consistently punished similar conduct.

debates.question: Did the Hunter Commission deliver justice?
debates.hook: An inquiry can name a failure and still leave the structure that produced it untouched. The question is whether that counts as justice.
debates.stakes: Post-colonial states still use commissions of inquiry after state violence. Jallianwala is an early test of whether an inquiry protects the state or the public.
caseFor: The commission created a public record, heard testimony, and rejected the claim that the firing was a normal response to a riot.
It criticised Dyer's conduct and contributed to his removal from command and his bar from employment in India.
The report gave nationalists and later historians a documented account that could be cited against official denial.
caseAgainst: No one was prosecuted for murder; Dyer was never tried in a criminal court.
The commission's terms of reference and composition were controlled by the colonial state, and its findings did not lead to a formal apology or reparations.
The Empire continued to honour Dyer in parts of the British press, turning the inquiry into a debate about his motives rather than the dead.
debates.uncomfortable: The inquiry was not a cover-up in the simple sense. It told the truth, and the truth was not enough to produce a punishment.
debates.whatWouldChange: Evidence that the commission's findings led to a criminal prosecution, or that the families received a formal state remedy comparable to the harm.

debates.question: Did the massacre cause the non-cooperation movement?
debates.hook: The massacre is often treated as the moment the Congress turned toward mass politics. It was one cause among several, and the difference matters.
debates.stakes: If we make one atrocity the cause of a mass movement, we lose the slower political work that made the movement possible — and we make politics look like a reaction to violence rather than a contest over strategy.
caseFor: The massacre destroyed the credibility of the idea that the Raj could be reformed from within.
It gave Gandhi and the Congress a moral vocabulary that could reach people who had not been moved by constitutional argument.
The years after 1919 saw a rapid expansion of Congress organization and a turn toward boycott and non-payment.
caseAgainst: The Rowlatt Act, the Khilafat question, inflation and wartime hardship were already creating mass discontent before April 1919.
The Congress had been moving toward mass politics before the massacre, and Gandhi's technique was developed in South Africa and Champaran.
Non-cooperation was launched in 1920 and then suspended in 1922 after Chauri Chaura; its trajectory cannot be reduced to one event.
debates.uncomfortable: The massacre did not create Indian nationalism. It removed an excuse for trusting the Empire, which is a different and more precise claim.
debates.whatWouldChange: Evidence that Congress organization and mass participation did not change after April 1919, or that the non-cooperation programme was already fixed before the massacre.

debates.question: Should the site be a memorial or a political warning?
debates.hook: A memorial can honour the dead and still soften the argument. The design of the place decides which one it is.
debates.stakes: Every state that commits violence later builds a site to remember it. The question is whether the site asks visitors to grieve, to obey, or to ask who was responsible.
caseFor: The site preserves the wall, the well and the narrow exits as physical evidence; that evidence is harder to deny than a speech.
A memorial gives families and survivors a public place of recognition, which the colonial state refused.
The annual remembrance can keep the names and the political demand alive across generations.
caseAgainst: Official memorials often turn political violence into a national story of suffering, which can obscure the specific order and the specific officer.
Tourism and ceremony can make the site comfortable; a comfortable site is easier for a state to accept.
The families' demand for an apology and a remedy can be displaced by the aesthetics of remembrance.
debates.uncomfortable: The same British state that expressed deep regret in 2019 has never issued the formal apology the families asked for. A memorial can be both a wound and a substitute for repair.
debates.whatWouldChange: Evidence that the memorial's official interpretation names the order, the officer and the inquiry's failure, rather than only mourning the dead.

debates.question: Was armed resistance the right response?
debates.hook: Jallianwala produced both a mass non-violent movement and a long memory of armed revenge. The argument is not about courage; it is about strategy.
debates.stakes: The choice between armed and non-violent resistance shaped the independence movement, the costs it imposed, and the kind of state that followed.
caseFor: The Empire had just shown that legal protest could be met with 1,650 rounds; armed resistance offered a way to make the cost of occupation real.
Udham Singh's assassination of O'Dwyer became a powerful symbol that the perpetrators were not untouchable.
Colonial rule was itself founded on violence, so the claim that the colonized must always be non-violent can look like a demand for unilateral restraint.
caseAgainst: Mass non-cooperation built a broader coalition than small armed actions and made the Empire's violence visible to a global audience.
Armed actions gave the state a pretext for repression and often isolated revolutionaries from the mass movement.
The strategic question is not whether the oppressed have a right to resist, but which form of resistance can win and what it does to the society that wins.
debates.uncomfortable: The non-violent movement and the armed underground existed at the same time, often in the same political culture. The choice was never as clean as the textbooks make it.
debates.whatWouldChange: Evidence that armed actions produced mass mobilization at a scale comparable to non-cooperation, or that non-violent protest failed to impose political costs on the Raj.

debates.question: What does Britain owe today?
debates.hook: The centenary produced deep regret, not an apology. The gap is where the politics lives.
debates.stakes: If an atrocity has no continuing obligation, then 'never again' is a sentiment rather than a policy. If it does, the question becomes what a remedy looks like across generations.
caseFor: A formal apology would acknowledge that the killing was wrong in law and in fact, not merely regrettable.
The families and the site deserve material support for remembrance, education and records; an apology without a remedy is cheap.
The Empire's records and the inquiry's findings should be part of a shared public history, not a footnote in a British military archive.
caseAgainst: A formal apology can become a substitute for material repair, allowing the state to close the file with words.
Contemporary taxpayers are not individually responsible for 1919, and broad reparation claims can be politically endless.
The Indian state has its own unresolved obligations to the families and to the memory of other colonial-era violence.
debates.uncomfortable: The 2019 expression of regret was carefully calibrated to stop short of legal responsibility. The wording was not an accident.
debates.whatWouldChange: Evidence that the British state has accepted legal responsibility, funded a remedy, or opened its records without conditions; or evidence that the families themselves reject a formal apology as the goal.
